strengths: Novel application of learning-to-learn to zeroth-order LLM optimization with practical 'train once, reuse widely' motivation
Well-grounded theoretical analysis via Theorem 1 showing per-block variance adaptation improves convergence bounds under block-diagonal Hessian assumptions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 28 task-model combinations with thorough ablations, learning rate sensitivity analysis, and memory/time overhead quantification
Elegant technical design with minimal overhead: <3.4% computational cost, <2MB additional memory for OPT-30B, via compact per-block neural networks
Strong reproducibility support with detailed implementation details, clear hyperparameter specifications, and algorithm descriptions
Consistent empirical improvements: 82.1% task-model combinations outperform MeZO baseline with 2.5% average accuracy gain
weaknesses: Critical gap: cross-architecture generalization completely untested—only tested transfer within same model family (LLaMA variants). No evidence optimizer trained on LLaMA transfers to Qwen or OPT, contradicting the 'train once, reuse widely' vision central to the motivation
Block-diagonal Hessian assumption only approximately holds; no empirical validation of actual block-diagonality in tested models or sensitivity analysis when assumption is violated
Unjustified approximation during L2L training: gradient flow is blocked through finite-difference estimator to save memory, lacking theoretical analysis of impact on convergence

Questionable COPA dataset selection for L2L training based on 'smooth loss decrease' and 'fast cycles'—appears somewhat arbitrary; limited multi-dataset comparison (C.5 shows single-dataset sometimes outperforms, unexplained)

Improvement magnitudes modest with high variance: wide error bands in Figure 2 (especially WSC), several task-model pairs show minimal gains within noise; 82.1% is convergence speed metric, not final accuracy
Substantial L2L meta-training overhead despite 'one-time cost' framing: 2.4× normal fine-tuning time, ~51 min GPU time for OPT-30B; unclear if investment scales across realistic task distributions
Incomplete PertNN architecture analysis: fixed design (2-layer MLP, 64 units) across all blocks without ablations on depth, capacity, or sensitivity to design choices
Unfixed L2L hyperparameters (η₁=10⁻⁶, η₂=10⁻², ε=10⁻³, reset period) appear selected without justification or sensitivity analysis

Loose connection between theory and practice: Theorem 1 provides bounds under ideal assumptions, but method learns variances from compressed statistics (mean/variance); tightness of this connection unclear
Limited evaluation horizon: experiments use 10k-20k steps; generalization to longer training trajectories and potential optimizer drift unexplored

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 LLMs and 7 datasets with consistent improvements in convergence speed and final loss (82.1% win rate)
Practical 'train once, reuse widely' paradigm well-motivated by LLM supply chain structure and demonstrated to work across tasks and model derivatives
Memory-efficient design with negligible overhead (<2MB auxiliary networks, ~1.6-3.4% runtime overhead) makes the approach genuinely practical
Excellent learning rate robustness (Figure 3): achieves comparable performance at 10^-8 to 10^-7 where baselines fail, a valuable practical property
Well-organized presentation with clear motivation, thorough ablations, and comprehensive appendices with implementation details and hyperparameter grids
Clever use of block-diagonal Hessian structure to make L2L scalable; normalization scheme (fixing ||Σ_t||_F = d) is mathematically justified
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 only proves block-wise variances *could* be better (existence), not that learning will find them. No guarantee that gradient descent on ω approaches theoretically optimal σ_j values. Theorem presented informally; gap between informal and formal (Theorem 3) statements unclear.

Significant implementation approximation under-discussed: Gradient flow blocking during L2L training (Section B.3) cuts loss gradients to save memory, substantially approximating the meta-learning objective. Only justified pragmatically, with no analysis of impact on optimizer quality. Buried in appendix despite being critical.

Unverified core assumption: Block-diagonal Hessian assumption is critical but never empirically validated for tested models/tasks. No analysis of off-diagonal block magnitudes or their impact on theoretical bounds.

Overstated generalization claims: (1) Single COPA training tested on only 7 similar tasks (text classification, NLI, QA), not diverse task types; (2) Only one derivative model test (LLaMA-3.1-8B → -Instruct); (3) Multi-dataset training no better than single-dataset (Fig 6), suggesting learned patterns are task-agnostic, not truly generalizing.

Modest empirical improvements for a top venue: 2.5% average accuracy improvement with 25% failure rate (only 75% task-model pairs show accuracy wins). Inconsistent with presented claims of 'strong performance'.

Methodological concerns: (1) Unfair hyperparameter comparison—MeZO-Adam grid is {1e-4 to 1e-6}, others {1e-6 to 1e-8}; (2) MeZO-Adam replaced with MeZO-AdamU for larger models without justification; (3) Auxiliary network architecture (2-layer, 64 units) unjustified—no ablation on depth/width or justification for this choice.

Design choices appear ad-hoc: Periodic reset mechanism lacks principled frequency selection; appears dataset-dependent. Per-block MLP architecture not validated against alternatives. No analysis of learned variances or their correlation with theory.

Incomplete experimental scope: Only small-scale downstream tasks (GLUE, SuperGLUE); no instruction tuning or generation quality. No comparison to LoRA or modern PEFT approaches—only other ZO methods. This is a significant omission for practical positioning.

Critical implementation details missing from main paper: Meta-training cost (Table 8: 51 min for OPT-30B, 332GB memory) relegated to appendix despite being substantial overhead. Reset frequency never formally specified. Gradient blocking approximation buried despite being a major approximation.

Reproducibility gaps: No variance analysis across multiple L2L training runs. Hyperparameter choices (η1, η2, reset period) lack justification. No mention of random seed/determinism. Auxiliary network capacity not ablated, making it unclear if architecture is a limiting factor.

strengths: Well-motivated approach combining learning-to-learn with zeroth-order optimization, grounded in block-diagonal Hessian structure of LLMs
Comprehensive experimental validation across 28 task-model pairs (4 LLMs, 7 datasets) with consistent improvements (82.1% win rate on converged loss)
Impressive cross-dataset and cross-derivative generalization: single-dataset training on COPA generalizes to 6 other datasets and model variants
Practical and memory-efficient design with minimal overhead (<2MB auxiliary networks for OPT-30B), making L2L feasible at LLM scale
Strong learning rate robustness across wide range (10^-8 to 10^-6), indicating adaptive optimization outperforms manually-tuned baselines
Thorough ablation studies validating design choices (normalization, periodic reset, parameter sharing strategy)
High reproducibility standards with detailed implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 1-3 are relatively straightforward extensions of existing MeZO analysis without convergence guarantees or formal rates
Modest empirical improvements: While 82.1% win rate sounds strong, individual task improvements are often 1-3% in accuracy (Table 1), averaging 2.5%
High L2L training cost (2.4× standard fine-tuning, 332GB memory, 51 min for OPT-30B) with unclear cost-benefit analysis; practical adoption requires model provider coordination
Limited generalization testing: only single-dataset training evaluated; only one model derivative tested; no evaluation across completely different architectures
Technical compromise not fully justified: gradient flow cutting through finite-difference term during L2L training is undocumented approximation without ablation studies
Block partitioning scheme not clearly specified ('natural parameter groups') despite being critical for reproducibility and Hessian-alignment
Missing analysis of learned optimizer: no visualization of learned variances, no investigation of task/model invariance, no failure mode analysis
Design choices lack principled justification: periodic reset addresses overfitting but appears ad-hoc; COPA selection criterion is informal

strengths: Well-motivated practical approach: The observation that a small set of base LLMs are repeatedly fine-tuned across tasks is compelling, and the 'train once, reuse widely' paradigm is practically valuable
Theoretically grounded with block-diagonal Hessian justification: Theorem 3.1 provides principled motivation for block-wise variance learning based on Transformer curvature structure
Clever scalable design with minimal overhead: Per-parameter-block lightweight MLPs achieve negligible memory (<2MB for OPT-30B) and time overhead (<3.4%) while enabling learned optimization

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Systematic evaluation on 4 LLMs and 7 datasets with strong baselines, extensive ablations, learning rate sensitivity analysis, and generalization tests across derivative checkpoints and longer-sequence tasks
Strong generalization: Single optimizer trained on COPA transfers reliably to other datasets and model variants, outperforming baselines in 82.1% of combinations
Excellent reproducibility: Extensive implementation details, hyperparameter grids, multiple ablations, and promised code release facilitate reproducibility
Robust to hyperparameter choices: Learning rate sensitivity analysis demonstrates the method is more robust than baselines across a wide range of learning rates
weaknesses: Informal theoretical justification: Theorem 3.1 provides upper bound improvement but relies on approximate block-diagonal Hessian assumption; no convergence guarantees provided, and gap between idealized theory and practice is unexplored

Missing cost-benefit analysis: Meta-training requires significant resources (332GB memory, 51 minutes for OPT-30B). Paper does not analyze breakeven point—how many downstream tasks justify this one-time cost? Critical for practitioners

Generalization mechanisms poorly understood: While empirical generalization is shown, why task-agnostic statistics (Mean, Var) transfer across fundamentally different tasks is unclear. Surprisingly, multi-dataset L2L training provides no substantial advantage (Section C.5), suggesting the optimizer doesn't learn deep task structure

Significant approximations under-analyzed: Gradient flow is cut off through the finite-difference term during L2L training to save memory (Appendix B.3). This substantial approximation affects optimizer learning but is dismissed with only 'strong empirical performance' mentioned; no ablation provided

Limited comparison with practical alternatives: Only compares against other zeroth-order methods; missing comparison with L2L baselines and no principled analysis of when ZO Fine-tuner is preferable to LoRA+quantization, which can also achieve low memory

Block-wise granularity not fully justified: Why Transformer parameter-blocks are the right unit is assumed rather than validated. No exploration of finer-grained (per-head) or coarser alternatives; effectiveness may be architecture-specific

Periodic reset mechanism appears ad-hoc: Resetting model parameters to address chronological bias in training data lacks principled justification. No ablations on reset frequency or exploration of alternative solutions (e.g., importance weighting)
Modest improvements in absolute terms: 2.5% average accuracy improvement and ~2.5% loss improvement are useful but incremental; gap to first-order methods remains (93% FO vs 92% ZO on some tasks)
Limited failure case analysis: Minimal improvements on WSC and other tasks; no analysis of failure modes or when task-specific optimization might be necessary

Incomplete L2L hyperparameter transparency: Section C.8 mentions tuning ε, η₁, η₂, reset schedule 'based on first-order trajectory behavior' but sensitivity to these choices and per-model tuning requirements are unclear

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 28 task-model pairs with consistent improvements (82.1% of combinations)
Well-motivated block-wise perturbation design justified by Hessian structure and practical LLM properties
Excellent engineering: minimal memory overhead (<2MB for OPT-30B) and time overhead (<3.4%)
Strong generalization: single optimizer trained on COPA transfers to diverse tasks and model derivatives
Thorough ablations and robustness analysis (learning rate sensitivity, design choices)
Clear presentation with reproducible implementation details and promised code release
weaknesses: Incremental improvements: average 2.5% accuracy gain without statistical significance testing; many individual tasks show negligible improvements
Limited theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.1 is straightforward and the block-diagonal Hessian assumption is not empirically verified for tested models
Gradient flow approximation (cutting off gradients through finite-difference estimator) lacks justification and ablation studies quantifying its impact
Overfitting to meta-training dataset: largest improvements appear on COPA (the training set); generalization to out-of-distribution tasks unclear
Generalization scope too narrow: all experiments on similar Transformer architectures (LLaMA, Qwen, OPT); no cross-architecture validation
Novelty concerns: L2L for optimization and even L2L for ZO (Ruan et al., 2020) are established; main contribution is block-wise scaling, which is somewhat incremental
Missing critical analyses: no statistical significance tests, no validation of block-diagonal Hessian assumption, no comparison with other learned optimizer approaches
Meta-training cost understated: requires 2.4× standard training time (3-51 minutes per model); break-even analysis with downstream tasks missing
Code unavailability: GitHub URL redacted, hindering reproducibility despite detailed documentation

strengths: Well-motivated practical approach leveraging the observation that most LLM checkpoints derive from few base models, enabling 'train once, reuse widely' paradigm that could influence deployment practice
Theoretically grounded: Theorem 3.1 provides principled justification for block-wise perturbation adaptation leveraging block-diagonal Hessian structure, building rigorously on MeZO analysis
Remarkably memory-efficient design with <2MB overhead per auxiliary network relative to 60GB models; elegant normalization technique decoupling variance from learning rate control

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 LLMs and 7 diverse NLP tasks (28 combinations) with strong results: 82.1% win rate in converged loss, 2.5% mean accuracy improvement, extensive ablations validating each component

Impressive out-of-distribution generalization: optimizer trained on COPA transfers consistently across dissimilar tasks (QA, sentiment, reasoning, coreference) and model derivatives with no task-specific tuning
Demonstrates superior learning rate robustness compared to baselines (Figure 3), achieving at 1×10⁻⁸ learning rates where MeZO fails—practical advantage for practitioners
Transparent implementation with detailed hyperparameter grids, algorithmic descriptions, component-wise runtime analysis, and reproducibility commitments (code and checkpoints)
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.1 guarantees tighter bounds only if σᵢ's perfectly match block-wise Hessian structure, but provides no analysis of whether the learned network actually captures this—no correlation study between learned variances and Hessian properties

L2L training complexity: Algorithm 2 combines multiple heuristic design choices (periodic resets tuned per-model, gradient-flow blocking approximation, empirical learning rates η₁/η₂); training costs 2.4× standard FO fine-tuning; gradient-blocking impact not ablated

Limited insight into learned representations: No visualization or interpretation of what perturbation variance patterns the network learns; makes it difficult to understand transferability mechanism or verify alignment with theoretical predictions

Generalization claims somewhat overstated: Evaluation confined to similar-distribution GLUE/SuperGLUE tasks; single MetaMathQA experiment is insufficient for strong out-of-distribution claims; Section C.5 shows single-dataset ≈ multi-dataset training, weakening 'one task suffices' narrative

Missing statistical significance testing: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite some improvements being modest (e.g., Table 1 accuracy differences <1%); Figure 2 shaded regions reflect curve smoothing, not model variance

Incomplete context: Notable gap to first-order methods (Appendix C.7, e.g., SQuAD 0.80 vs 0.82) not discussed; no consideration of combining with parameter-efficient methods (LoRA, QLoRA) that are practical standard; scope limited to decoder-only Transformers and NLP

Reproducibility concerns despite promises: Multiple L2L tuning choices appear heuristic (COPA selection rationale informal; reset schedule tuning basis unclear); 'fixed-seed scripts' promised but not provided; fairness concern: Table 7 claims minimal hyperparameters but excludes L2L tuning costs

Gap between informal and formal theory: Theorem D.5 invokes 'ideal situation' without precise definition; block-diagonal assumption is 'approximate' but off-diagonal error quantification is informal, not rigorously bounded
